title: Cuban Missile Crisis: 13 Days on the Brink of Nuclear War
alt_titles: The Cuban Missile Crisis, Day by Day
How the World Almost Ended in October 1962
The Secret Deal That Ended the Cuban Missile Crisis
thumbnail_file: U-2 photo during Cuban Missile Crisis.jpg
description_summary: In October 1962, an American spy plane found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 90 miles from Florida. This is the story of the thirteen days that followed: the quarantine, Black Saturday, the secret Turkey deal, and why the famous 'eyeball to eyeball' moment never really happened.

scenes.narration: On the morning of Tuesday the sixteenth of October 1962, President John F. Kennedy was shown a set of photographs. They had been taken by a spy plane flying high over Cuba, just ninety miles from Florida. They showed Soviet nuclear missile sites being built. The photos had been taken two days earlier. Cuba was an ally of the Soviet Union.

For the next thirteen days, the world came closer to nuclear war than at any other time. American and Soviet forces were placed on high alert. Warships faced each other at sea. And the two leaders tried to find a way out before someone made a fatal mistake. Millions of people followed the news with growing fear.

This is the story of those thirteen days. It covers how the missiles got there, how the crisis was resolved, and a secret deal that stayed hidden for decades. It also explains why one of its most famous moments never really happened.

shots.file: File:U-2 photo during Cuban Missile Crisis.jpg
shots.caption: A U-2 photo of a missile site in Cuba, October 1962
How far the missiles in Cuba could reach

scenes.narration: In 1959, Fidel Castro's revolutionaries took power in Cuba. His government grew close to the Soviet Union. In April 1961, a CIA-backed force of Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs, hoping to overthrow him. The invasion failed within days. Castro feared another attempt would follow.

shots.caption: Fidel Castro

card.text: The Bay of Pigs invasion fails

scenes.narration: The Soviet leader, Nikita Khrushchev, had his own concerns. In 1961, the United States had placed Jupiter nuclear missiles in Italy and Turkey, within range of the Soviet Union. Khrushchev wanted to protect his new ally and even the balance.

shots.caption: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev
An American Jupiter missile, the type based in Turkey

scenes.narration: In the summer of 1962, he approved a secret plan, code-named Anadyr. Soviet ships would carry nuclear missiles and tens of thousands of troops to Cuba. Much of it was hidden below deck, out of sight of American spy planes.

shots.file: File:Soviet freighter Krasnograd steams for Cuba in September 1962.jpg
shots.caption: A Soviet freighter heading for Cuba, September 1962

card.label: Soviet troops eventually sent to Cuba

scenes.narration: On the fourteenth of October, an American U-2 spy plane flown by Major Richard Heyser passed over western Cuba. Its cameras took more than nine hundred photographs. The next day, analysts spotted something alarming near the town of San Cristóbal. They compared it with photos of known Soviet missile bases.

shots.caption: A Lockheed U-2 spy plane

card.label: Photos taken on the U-2 flight

scenes.narration: The pictures showed medium-range ballistic missiles. They could reach about two thousand kilometres, far enough to hit much of the eastern United States, including Washington. Later flights found sites for longer-range missiles too. The first missiles had arrived only weeks earlier.

shots.file: File:The relative ranges of the IL-28, SS-4, and SS-5, stationed on Cuba.png
shots.caption: Ranges of the Soviet weapons in Cuba

card.label: Range of the medium-range missiles
card.note: SS-4, also known as the R-12

shots.caption: Reconnaissance photo of Soviet missile equipment in Cuba

scenes.narration: On the morning of the sixteenth, Kennedy was told. He gathered a small group of senior advisers, later known as ExComm. They met in secret that evening. Meanwhile, the president kept to his normal schedule. He did not want the Soviets to realise the missiles had been found.

shots.file: File:Meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Security Council- Cuba Crisis. President Kennedy, Secretary of... - NARA - 194246.jpg
shots.caption: Kennedy's advisers, known as ExComm, in session

scenes.narration: The advisers argued for days. Some, including military chiefs, wanted air strikes on the missile sites, followed by an invasion of Cuba. Others warned that attacking could kill Soviet troops and trigger war in Europe or worse.

shots.caption: Kennedy with Air Force chief Curtis LeMay

scenes.narration: On the eighteenth, Kennedy met the Soviet foreign minister, Andrei Gromyko. Gromyko insisted there were no offensive weapons in Cuba. Kennedy did not reveal what he knew. It was a test of nerve on both sides.

By the twenty first, Kennedy had decided on a naval blockade to stop more weapons reaching Cuba. He called it a quarantine, partly because a blockade was legally an act of war. It would give Khrushchev time to back down.

shots.file: File:President Kennedy - signing Cuba Quarantine Proclamation.jpg
shots.caption: Kennedy signs the quarantine order, 23 October 1962

scenes.narration: At seven in the evening on Monday the twenty second, Kennedy went on television. He told the nation about the missiles, announced the quarantine and demanded their removal. He warned that any missile launched from Cuba would be met with a full response against the Soviet Union.

American forces worldwide moved to a higher state of alert. Bombers carrying nuclear weapons took to the air. In Cuba, Castro mobilised his armed forces. The next day, the Organization of American States backed the quarantine. Khrushchev called it an act of piracy.

card.text: Latin American states back the quarantine

shots.caption: US forces enforcing the quarantine, 1962

scenes.narration: The quarantine began on Wednesday the twenty fourth. Soviet ships were heading for the line, and Soviet submarines were in the area. Any ship that reached the line could be stopped and searched. In Washington, advisers waited for news of the first confrontation.

shots.file: File:Location of Navy and Soviet ships during the Cuban Missile Crisis.jpg
shots.caption: US Navy and Soviet ships during the crisis

shots.file: File:P-2H Neptune over Soviet ship Oct 1962.jpg
shots.query: US Navy plane over Soviet ship 1962
shots.caption: A US Navy patrol plane over a Soviet ship

scenes.narration: That morning, word came that Soviet ships had stopped or turned around. At the White House, the tension broke for a moment. Secretary of State Dean Rusk is said to have remarked, we're eyeball to eyeball, and the other fellow just blinked. It became the most famous line of the crisis. Kennedy's advisers later retold it in books and memoirs, and it even appears in films.

card.text: We're eyeball to eyeball, and the other fellow just blinked.

scenes.narration: But the historian Michael Dobbs found that the drama never happened as told. The Soviet missile ships had turned back on Khrushchev's orders about thirty hours earlier. When Rusk spoke, they were about five hundred miles from the line, heading home. American intelligence learned this within hours.

card.label: How far the missile ships were from the line

scenes.narration: The missiles already in Cuba were still there, and work on the sites continued. On the twenty fifth, the US ambassador Adlai Stevenson confronted his Soviet counterpart at the United Nations, showing the spy-plane photos to the world. American forces were raised to DEFCON 2, one step short of nuclear war.

shots.file: File:Adlai Stevenson shows missiles to UN Security Council with David Parker standing.jpg
shots.caption: Adlai Stevenson shows the photos to the UN, 25 October 1962

card.label: The highest US alert level ever reached

shots.caption: A medium-range missile site, 25 October 1962

scenes.narration: On Friday the twenty sixth, a long letter arrived from Khrushchev. He offered to remove the missiles if the United States promised never to invade Cuba. It looked like a way out. Then, the next morning, a second message arrived.

Broadcast on Radio Moscow, the second message added a new demand: the United States must also remove its missiles from Turkey. That same Saturday, an American U-2 was shot down over Cuba by a Soviet missile. Its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, was killed. He was the only person killed by enemy fire during the crisis.

card.text: A U-2 is shot down over Cuba

shots.caption: Major Rudolf Anderson

scenes.narration: Under the sea, US warships dropped practice depth charges to force a Soviet submarine, B-59, to surface. Its crew did not know that the charges were only signals. Survivors later described stifling heat as the batteries ran low. The submarine carried a nuclear torpedo. One senior officer, Vasily Arkhipov, refused to agree to launch it.

shots.caption: The Soviet submarine B-59, forced to surface

card.label: Officer who refused to approve a nuclear launch

scenes.narration: That evening, Robert Kennedy met the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, in secret. He warned that time was running out. He also said that the missiles in Turkey would be removed after the crisis. But this part of the deal must never be made public.

At nine o'clock on the morning of Sunday the twenty eighth, Washington time, Radio Moscow broadcast Khrushchev's reply. The Soviet Union would dismantle the missiles and take them home. Kennedy welcomed it as a statesmanlike decision. Both leaders had stepped back from the edge.

card.label: Khrushchev agrees to remove the missiles

scenes.narration: In public, the deal was simple. The missiles would leave Cuba under UN observation, and the United States would not invade. The American Jupiter missiles in Turkey were quietly removed within months. That part stayed secret for more than twenty five years.

shots.caption: A site being dismantled, 1 November 1962

card.text: The Turkey part of the deal

shots.file: File:EXCOMM meeting, Cuban Missile Crisis, 29 October 1962.jpg
shots.caption: An ExComm meeting, 29 October 1962

scenes.narration: The crisis did not end at once. Arguments continued over Soviet bombers that had also been sent to Cuba. When Khrushchev agreed to withdraw them, Kennedy lifted the quarantine in November. American planes photographed the missiles being loaded back onto ships.

shots.caption: Missile site photographed on 17 October 1962

scenes.narration: Both sides had been shaken by how close they had come. In 1963, they set up a direct teletype link between Washington and Moscow, known as the hotline, so the leaders could communicate quickly. That summer, they agreed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere.

Within two years, both leaders were gone. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas in November 1963. Khrushchev was removed from power by his own colleagues in October 1964. Many in Moscow felt he had backed down over Cuba. Castro, too, was angry that he had not been consulted about the deal.

The Cuban Missile Crisis was not won by one side staring the other down. It ended because both leaders looked for a way out, and offered each other a compromise. The world came very close to nuclear war, and learned from it. Sources and image credits are in the description.
